extracted.intended_audience: USPTO-registered patent and trademark practitioners, counsel, and respondents in USPTO disciplinary matters
extracted.subtask_short: USPTO practitioner conduct and signature rules
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements governing how practitioners must sign, certify, supervise, and present trademark and patent papers to the USPTO (including S-signatures, micro entity certifications, reasonable inquiry obligations, supervision of non-practitioner assistants), and the sanctions/monitoring conditions for violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature requirements (37 C.F.R. § 2.193)
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures on trademark documents must be signed by a proper person; trademark documents must be personally signed by the signatory named on the document; a person electronically signing a document must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces, and/or punctuation marks adopted as a signature and place that combination between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP § 611.01(c) emphasizes: the person identified as the signatory must personally sign the printed form or personally enter his or her electronic signature; another person (e.g., paralegal, assistant) may not sign or enter the name of a qualified U.S. attorney or other authorized signatory. "Typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature by that person."

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of impermissible trademark signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: If the signature on a trademark application or other submission fails to comply with 37 C.F.R. § 2.193 because it was entered by someone other than the named signatory or not signed by a proper person, the submission is improperly executed, cannot be relied upon to support registration, and normally renders the application void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order cites authorities and the 84 Fed. Reg. statement that an improper signatory may invalidate a registration; trademark application declarations are signed under penalty of perjury and false statements may implicate 18 U.S.C. § 1001.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent signature requirements and originals (37 C.F.R. § 1.4(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Each piece of correspondence requiring a person's signature must be an original with an original handwritten signature personally signed in permanent dark ink, or be a direct/indirect copy (photocopy/facsimile) of an original (which should be retained as evidence of authenticity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a copy of the original is filed, the original should be retained; the Office may require submission of the original if authenticity is questioned. Handwritten signatures are preferred except where S-signature rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: S-signature rules for patent filings (37 C.F.R. § 1.4(d)(2)-(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: An S-signature is a signature inserted between forward slash marks and includes signatures made by electronic or mechanical means (not a handwritten signature). For patent correspondence, an S-signature may be used instead of a handwritten signature subject to specific requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements include: (i) S-signature must consist only of letters or Arabic numerals (with appropriate spaces and common punctuation) and be inserted between single forward slashes (e.g., /Dr. James T. Jones, Jr/); (ii) a patent practitioner must supply his/her registration number as part of or adjacent to the S-signature; (iii) signer's name must be presented in printed or typed form immediately below or adjacent and reasonably specific so identity is recognizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro entity certification timing and formalities (37 C.F.R. § 1.29; MPEP § 509.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants claiming reduced fees as a micro entity must establish micro entity status by filing a written certification prior to or at the time a fee is first paid in the micro entity amount; fee may be paid in micro entity amount only if submitted with or subsequent to the certification of entitlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 509.04 provides procedure guidance; failing to timely or properly file the certification can result in Notices of Missing Parts or Notices of Payment Deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud prohibition for micro entity claims (37 C.F.R. § 1.29(j))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Any attempt to fraudulently establish status or pay fees as a micro entity shall be considered as a fraud practiced or attempted on the Office. Improperly, and with intent to deceive, establishing status or paying fees as a micro entity shall be considered as a fraud practiced or attempted on the Office."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signing or presenting incorrect micro entity certifications (including knowingly claiming micro entity status when ineligible) may be treated as fraud on the Office and can trigger disciplinary or criminal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification obligations when presenting papers (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: By presenting any paper to the USPTO, the practitioner certifies that statements on his/her own knowledge are true, that statements made on information and belief are believed to be true, and that, to the best of the party's knowledge, information and belief formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances: (i) the paper is not for an improper purpose; (ii) legal contentions are warranted by existing law or nonfrivolous argument; (iii) allegations and factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to have such after investigation; and (iv) denials of factual contentions are warranted or reasonably based on lack of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2) sets out the four-prong certification; violations may jeopardize the probative value of filings and are subject to disciplinary action and potential criminal liability under 18 U.S.C. § 1001.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inquiry obligation (under § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must conduct an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances that supports the factual assertions set forth in any paper presented to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to perform a reasonable inquiry (e.g., relying exclusively on third-party representatives without verification) can violate § 11.18, undermine filings' probative value, and result in discipline; examples in the Final Order include not verifying that applicants actually signed documents or were eligible for micro entity status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.503(a),(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have responsibilities over non-practitioner assistants and must adequately supervise such assistants' activities connected to USPTO filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing non-practitioner assistants to review, sign (including signing practitioner's name), or file trademark or patent documents without adequate supervision or controls violates supervision rules. The Order cites permitting an assistant to operate in practitioner’s absence and to sign the practitioner’s name as examples of inadequate supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assisting unauthorized practice of law (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not assist another person in practicing law in a jurisdiction in violation of the laws or rules governing the legal profession of that jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include allowing foreign non-practitioner representatives to prepare legal responses, then permitting an assistant to sign and file those responses without practitioner review—thereby assisting unauthorized practice before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward the tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1),(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not knowingly make false statements of material fact to a tribunal or offer evidence the practitioner knows to be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions certifying that a named signatory signed a document when the practitioner knew they did not constitute violations. Candor obligations apply to both trademark and patent proceedings before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation in connection with practice before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting documents not signed by the named signatory or falsely certifying the truth of assertions are cited as examples of conduct meeting this prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to USPTO administration (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of the USPTO patent or trademark processes (e.g., practices that undermine the integrity of the registration or patent issuance systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing impermissibly signed submissions that may lead to invalid registrations or patents, failing to notify USPTO or clients about impermissible signatures, and failing to have adequate controls are provided as examples of prejudicial conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must provide competent representation, which includes conducting reasonable inquiries under the circumstances, knowing and following applicable USPTO rules, and having adequate procedures to ensure filings comply with USPTO requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to know signature rules, to verify signatures or micro entity eligibility, or to have reasonable procedures to corroborate relied-on information are cited as competence failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and promptness in representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence and promptness, including timely informing clients of issues and taking reasonable steps to ensure filings are complete and accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failures include not timely informing clients of impermissible signatures or potential adverse consequences and filing documents with missing information that prompt Notices of Missing Parts or Incomplete Replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client communication and explanation (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must keep clients reasonably informed about the status of matters and explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit informed client decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delaying or failing to inform clients about signature requirements or the potential consequences of impermissible signatures violates these obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention and authenticity of original signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: When a copy of an original handwritten signature is filed (e.g., scanned into PDF), the original should be retained as evidence of authenticity and the Office may require submission of the original if authenticity is questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order notes instances where handwritten signatures scanned into PDFs were provided by third parties and the practitioner did not ensure authenticity—this failure is noted as problematic under signature rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial duties after discovering impermissible signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who discover they presented impermissibly signed trademark or patent documents must conduct an in-depth review, inform the USPTO offices (Trademark Policy or Patent Legal Administration) in writing of each such document, and provide written notification to affected clients or inventors about actual or potential harm to their IP rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent represented that he conducted reviews and provided written notifications; the Final Order requires such remediation as part of discipline and monitors remediation steps as an element of compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and restrictions framework for misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary consequences may include suspension from practice before the USPTO, probation with conditions, limited recognition for a short period to conclude pending matters, restrictions on USPTO account access, obligations to cooperate in investigations, and potential additional suspension for probation violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this Final Order the practitioner was suspended for 14 months, subject to probation beginning on reinstatement, limited 30-day recognition to conclude matters, prohibited from applying for/using USPTO verified accounts until reinstated, and required to cooperate with inquiries into related foreign entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation monitoring and reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions while on probation can include mandated searches and reporting (e.g., bi-weekly searches of USPTO trademark system to identify filings naming the practitioner as attorney of record and prompt notice to USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy), bi-monthly written reports to OED Director of search results, and requirement to have practice monitors who audit filings quarterly and file reports to the OED Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice monitors must meet specified qualifications (Trademark Practice Monitor: attorney in good standing with 5+ years USPTO trademark practice; Patent Practice Monitor: USPTO-registered practitioner with 5+ years patent practice); monitors must audit a reasonable number of filings, identify specific problematic filings, make suggestions to improve processes, and file initial and subsequent reports on a set 91/90 day cadence. Failure to ensure timely monitor reports can trigger show-cause proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice monitor confidentiality and cost responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice monitors viewing confidential client information must understand and agree to maintain confidentiality under 37 C.F.R. § 11.106; the respondent/practitioner is responsible for paying all costs, expenses, and any fees of the practice monitor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order requires respondent to ensure practice monitors agree to confidentiality and imposes financial responsibility for monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing legal education (CLE) requirement for reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of reinstatement to practice before the USPTO, the respondent must provide a declaration that he has successfully completed six (6) hours of CLE credit on ethics/professional responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CLE is explicitly tied to reinstatement and is part of the required remediation of professional competence/ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on USPTO electronic account usage during suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: While suspended and until reinstated, the practitioner is prohibited from applying for or obtaining a USPTO verified Electronic System account, having his name added to one, opening/activating USPTO.gov accounts for filing, verifying others' credentials for such accounts, or sponsoring such accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO is authorized to disable or suspend the practitioner's USPTO.gov accounts; the practitioner bears responsibility to request re-activation after reinstatement if desired.
